solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Sour, very pure cream? (3-5)

blocks.note: milk that has gone off has turned sour
white stands for purity, as in whiter than white

annotation.surface: Someone complaining that the cream has turned, despite being sold as very pure.
annotation.walkthrough: Cream reads as the dairy product that goes sour; it is the pale colour. The question mark flags that shift.
annotation.definitionFit: Cream is a yellowish-white shade, one of the colours called off-white.

entries.clue: Loves record by soprano in X-Factor: ‘I am the Eggman!’ (8)

indicatorNotes.by: 'by' in its sense of 'next to', so the soprano chunk stands beside the record
indicatorNotes.in: the soprano sits inside the X-Factor

blocks.note: love = O, the zero score in tennis; two of them
a log is a written record
S is the standard abbreviation for soprano
the X factor is that indefinable something, 'it'

annotation.surface: A soprano contestant on The X Factor belting out the Beatles lyric from I Am the Walrus.
annotation.walkthrough: The X Factor is a TV talent show and 'I am the Eggman' a Beatles line, so the clue feels like pop trivia; the Eggman is taken literally as an egg collector.
annotation.definitionFit: An oologist studies or collects birds' eggs, so could fairly call himself the Eggman.

entries.clue: Surprisingly, a bionic fart is a man-made thing (11)

indicatorNotes.Surprisingly: the letters turn up in a surprising order

annotation.surface: A mock-serious observation that a robotic flatulence would be artificial.
annotation.walkthrough: A schoolboy-silly surface; the fodder is the whole middle of the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A fabrication is something made or constructed, hence a man-made thing.

entries.clue: Awfully rapid heat in which hot air will rise? (3,6)

annotation.definition: in which hot air will rise?
annotation.definitionNote: a descriptive phrase standing for the noun: the chart in which hot airs rise

indicatorNotes.Awfully: the letters are put together awfully, i.e. badly, so must be rearranged

annotation.surface: A physics lesson: fierce, fast heating makes hot air go up.
annotation.walkthrough: Hot air suggests convection, but an air is a tune: hot new songs climb the hit parade, the singles chart.
annotation.definitionFit: The hit parade is the chart of best-selling records, where popular tunes rise.

entries.clue: Concise poetry first released by tenor (5)

indicatorNotes.first released: the first letter is let go
indicatorNotes.by: 'by' in its sense of 'next to', so the tenor stands beside the shortened poetry

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for tenor

annotation.surface: A tenor putting out his new short collection of poems.
annotation.walkthrough: 'First released' sounds like a debut publication; here it strips the V from VERSE.
annotation.definitionFit: Terse means brief and to the point, i.e. concise.

entries.clue: Get old black and brown trousers close to Delhi (6)

indicatorNotes.trousers: as a verb: the brown pockets, i.e. holds inside it, the next letter
indicatorNotes.close to: the close of a word is its end, so this points at the final letter

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
B for black, as on pencils
the last letter of Delhi, placed inside TAN

annotation.surface: An instruction to buy some old-fashioned black and brown trousers near Delhi.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like clothing but is a verb here: to trouser is to pocket.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: you get a ticket or obtain one, the second just more formal.

entries.clue: Labour’s source of bottomless hilarity on leader’s exit (5)

indicatorNotes.source of: the source of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: A political jibe: the Labour party provides endless laughs once its leader quits.
annotation.walkthrough: Labour looks like the party; it is childbirth. 'Bottomless' is not an adjective on hilarity but the word giving B.
annotation.definitionFit: Labour ends in birth, and the two are used as near-synonyms for delivering a baby.

entries.clue: Is your setter to produce china in France? (3)

blocks.note: the verb 'is' as the setter would say it of himself
the setter refers to himself as I

annotation.surface: The setter wondering whether he could make porcelain in France.
annotation.walkthrough: China is Cockney rhyming slang for mate (china plate = mate), and ami is French for friend; the surface leans on the crockery sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Ami is the French word for friend, which china means in rhyming slang.

entries.clue: I’m going to crash in the darkness (5)

blocks.note: to crash is slang for going to sleep; think of the clipped word you call out as you head to bed
the dark hours between sunset and dawn

annotation.surface: Someone warning that they are about to drive into something because they cannot see.
annotation.walkthrough: Crash reads as a collision; it is slang for going to sleep, and 'Night!' is short for goodnight.
annotation.definitionFit: Night means the hours of darkness, and 'Night!' is the parting word before bed.

entries.clue: A military installation worried deserter (8)

blocks.note: as in 'what's eating you?': ate = worried

annotation.surface: An anxious army deserter at a base.
annotation.walkthrough: The military surface makes deserter look like a runaway soldier; an apostate deserts a faith or cause.
annotation.definitionFit: An apostate abandons their religion or party, a deserter of belief.

entries.clue: One can pinch bishop skewering misplaced queen (7)

indicatorNotes.skewering: B is driven through the middle of LOST, like a skewer

blocks.note: B is the chess notation for bishop

annotation.surface: A chess move: a bishop attacking through a queen that has been badly placed.
annotation.walkthrough: Bishop and queen suggest chess, but the definition is a creature with claws.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the lobster is known for its pincer claws, and 'One can pinch' also hints at a thief, the sense the surface avoids.

entries.clue: Barnet intersection? (7)

blocks.note: not the London borough but rhyming slang for hair (Barnet Fair = hair)
not a road junction but the line where something is cut in two

annotation.surface: A road junction in Barnet, a borough of north London.
annotation.walkthrough: Barnet is a London borough, but also Cockney rhyming slang for hair (Barnet Fair = hair); the line dividing hair is a parting.
annotation.definitionFit: A parting is where hair is split into two sides, a crossing line through the barnet.

entries.clue: Producers of The Faces run into stern maestros (9)

indicatorNotes.into: 'into' means entering, so the run goes inside the maestros

blocks.note: R for run, as in cricket scoring

annotation.surface: Record producers who worked with the Faces, the 1970s rock band, joining a strict group of maestros.
annotation.walkthrough: The Faces were a British rock band, so 'producers' looks musical; people who make faces are grimacers.
annotation.definitionFit: Grimacers pull faces, so they literally produce faces.

entries.clue: Work put into successful release Get Out (3,2)

indicatorNotes.put into: to be put into something is to be placed within it, so the work sits inside the release

annotation.surface: Promoting the horror film Get Out, a successful release.
annotation.walkthrough: Get Out looks like the film title; 'hop it' is British slang for go away.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Hop it!' is a brusque British way of saying get out.

entries.clue: Plasterers plastered plastering top of nursery alone? (11)

indicatorNotes.plastered: drunk, so the letters stagger into a new order
indicatorNotes.plastering: covering, so the fodder takes the N in with it
indicatorNotes.top of: the first letter of a down-read word

blocks.note: first letter of nursery, added to the fodder

annotation.surface: Drunken plasterers doing up a nursery on their own.
annotation.walkthrough: Three plaster words in a row make the surface; the first is fodder, the second means drunk, the third means covering.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: without a partner at a dance or in life, you are on your own.

entries.clue: Sierra, Hotel, Alpha, Kilo, Alpha and Zulu? (5)

blocks.note: each is a NATO phonetic alphabet code word, standing for its own initial letter

annotation.surface: A string of radio call signs from the NATO phonetic alphabet, ending with Zulu.
annotation.walkthrough: Zulu looks like just another letter of the alphabet (Z); it is the definition, since Shaka was the great Zulu king.
annotation.definitionFit: Shaka was a famous early-19th-century Zulu king, so he is a Zulu, as the question mark admits.

entries.clue: Fancy star pad filled with old screenwriters, perhaps (8)

indicatorNotes.Fancy: a fanciful arrangement of the letters
indicatorNotes.filled with: O is taken into the fodder

blocks.note: O for old, added to the fodder

annotation.surface: A luxurious celebrity apartment full of veteran Hollywood writers.
annotation.walkthrough: Screenwriters who turn novels into films are adaptors; 'perhaps' marks them as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: Screenwriters often adapt books or plays for film, making them adaptors.

entries.clue: One who’ll help a female unionist in hearing (8)

indicatorNotes.in hearing: what the ear takes in, not the spelling

blocks.note: trade unionists call each other brother and sister

annotation.surface: A union helper sitting in on a disciplinary hearing.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'hearing' suggests a tribunal; it is the sound signal. Union members address each other as brother and sister.
annotation.definitionFit: An assister is simply someone who assists, one who'll help.

entries.clue: Gentle record by The Police turned up by judge (9)

indicatorNotes.turned up: in a down entry, turning up reads the letters bottom to top

blocks.note: an EP is an extended-play record

annotation.surface: A mellow record by the band The Police, turned up loud by a judge.
annotation.walkthrough: The Police are also a rock band, so 'record by The Police' feels musical; here it means the London force, the Met.
annotation.definitionFit: Temperate means mild or moderate, i.e. gentle.

entries.clue: Take it easy if son gets doubly depressed (4,4)

annotation.surface: Advice to relax when your son becomes seriously depressed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doubly' asks for two different words meaning depressed, LOW then DOWN.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for an idiom: both phrasal verbs mean easing off the pace of work or life.

entries.clue: During class, popular European flicks admirer (8)

indicatorNotes.During: the next letters sit within the time, i.e. inside, CASTE

annotation.surface: A student in class flicking notes to a European admirer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flicks' looks like a verb; it is the informal noun for films.
annotation.definitionFit: A borrowing from French for a film buff; 'the flicks' is old informal British for the cinema, from the flickering picture.

entries.clue: Patch of cream on a large pheasant (5)

indicatorNotes.Patch of: a small part of the following words

annotation.surface: A cream-coloured marking on a big pheasant's plumage.
annotation.walkthrough: The plumage surface hides the answer in plain view; a monal is a Himalayan pheasant.
annotation.definitionFit: The monal is a brightly coloured Himalayan pheasant.

entries.clue: Way in which commando leader produces weapon (5)

indicatorNotes.in which: the way has the next letter inside it
indicatorNotes.leader: the leader of a word is the letter at its head, its first

annotation.surface: A route by which a commando chief makes a weapon.
annotation.walkthrough: The military surface fits weapon; the commando only supplies its initial.
annotation.definitionFit: A lance is a long spear carried by mounted soldiers.

entries.clue: Go and throw up after husband turns 50 (5)

indicatorNotes.turns: 'turns' in the sense of 'becomes', so the husband letter becomes the 50 letter

blocks.note: L is the Roman numeral for 50, replacing the H

annotation.surface: A husband turning 50, feeling sick and wanting to leave.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turns 50' reads as a birthday; it means H becomes L.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'I must go' and 'I must leave' say the same thing.

entries.clue: After getting into drugs, staff deteriorate (5)

indicatorNotes.getting into: the staff goes inside the drugs

blocks.note: E = ecstasy; two of them for the plural

annotation.surface: Employees' performance declining after they get into drugs.
annotation.walkthrough: Staff looks like employees; it is a stick, ROD.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: rock wears away bit by bit, and so do standards or trust that are said to deteriorate.

entries.clue: Fieldworker perhaps in Orca’s crew at sea (9)

indicatorNotes.at sea: confused, so the letters are mixed

annotation.surface: A field researcher among the crew of the boat Orca, the shark hunters' vessel in Jaws.
annotation.walkthrough: The Orca is the boat in Jaws, so 'at sea' feels literal; a scarecrow works in a field.
annotation.definitionFit: A scarecrow does its job standing in a field, a fieldworker of sorts.

entries.clue: One with many branches in American resort (5)

blocks.note: not a chain of shops but a tree, here a kind of poplar
a fashionable ski town in Colorado

annotation.surface: A company with many branches operating in a US holiday town.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Many branches' sounds like a chain of shops; it is a tree.
annotation.definitionFit: An aspen is a poplar tree, and Aspen is a Colorado ski resort.

entries.clue: Fat daughter, one kept under wraps by a model (7)

indicatorNotes.kept under wraps by: something kept under wraps is covered up, so the wrapper goes round it

annotation.surface: A plump daughter being hidden away by a model.
annotation.walkthrough: Model reads as a person; it is the verb pose.
annotation.definitionFit: Adipose means fatty, as in adipose tissue.

entries.clue: Rocks I carefully evade at the front (3)

indicatorNotes.at the front: take the front letter of each word

annotation.surface: A sailor steering carefully around rocks at the bow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On the rocks' means with ice, so rocks is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Rocks is slang for ice cubes in a drink.

entries.clue: Put down contrary old boy, one acting as a dummy (7)

indicatorNotes.contrary: contrary means facing the opposite way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: OB = old boy, a former pupil

annotation.surface: Putting a stubborn old man in his place, as he plays the fool.
annotation.walkthrough: Dummy suggests a fool; here it is a dummy pill, which is what a placebo is.
annotation.definitionFit: A placebo is a dummy treatment with no active ingredient.

entries.clue: Piece from Liszt with energy in regular time? (6)

indicatorNotes.Piece from: one letter of Liszt, its first
indicatorNotes.in: plain 'in': the Liszt-and-energy pair is placed inside the word for regular

annotation.surface: A Liszt piece played energetically but in strict tempo.
annotation.walkthrough: The musical surface makes 'regular time' look like tempo; time is the definition, eleven being an hour.
annotation.definitionFit: Eleven is a time of day, as in eleven o'clock; the question mark admits it is one example.

entries.clue: Live at home with a child (2,6)

blocks.note: as in 'ten pounds a head': a = per

annotation.surface: Someone living at home with their child.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Live' reads as the verb to dwell; it is the adjective, as in a live performance.
annotation.definitionFit: A live appearance is one made in person rather than recorded.
